title: What Cain said to Abel
hookLine: Genesis Rabbah and other midrash fill the Torah's silences with stories
carry: midrash listens to the Torah's silences
last: THE SABBATH IS GIVEN TO YOU.

cards: Two brothers. One brings an offering and it's accepted. The other brings one and it isn't.
God warns the angry brother that sin is crouching at the door. Then the verse says Cain spoke to Abel his brother, and in the Hebrew, that's where the sentence stops. No words follow.
Next, they are in the field, and Cain rises up against Abel and kills him. Something was said, and it ended with a brother dead in a field. The text leaves it blank.
The sages leaned into that silence.

teach.b: Stories in the gaps. You met these brothers long ago; today is about what the sages heard in their silence.

It's this path's name for midrash that fills the Torah's silences with stories, and Genesis Rabbah, a collection of midrash on Genesis, is full of them. First, the gap. The Torah tells stories with very few words.
It rarely says what people thought, and sometimes, as with Cain, not even what they said. The sages treated those silences as places to stop and listen. Second, what Genesis Rabbah hears.

What were they arguing about? It offers more than one answer. In one, the brothers divide the world: one takes the land, the other everything that moves, and soon each is telling the other to get off his property.
In another, they argue over whose territory will hold the holy Temple. In another, the quarrel is over a woman.
Third, the midrash doesn't choose. It sets the answers side by side, each a different picture of how brothers come to violence. The silence stays open, now with voices in it.
Fourth, a story in the gaps isn't meant to replace the verse. The verse still says what it says, and still stops where it stops.
The midrash is a reader saying: here is something this silence might hold, and why it matters to us. Yesterday, that close reading produced a law. Today it produces a story.

how: Jewish readers study midrash collections such as Genesis Rabbah alongside the weekly Torah portion, and teachers draw on its stories when they explain a passage. Rashi's commentary on the Torah also brings some of these midrashim to readers.

games.q: you're a sage reading 'Cain spoke to Abel', with no words after it. you've heard three explanations of the quarrel. what do you do with them?
o: choose the most likely one and drop the others.
set them side by side and keep them all.
say the text is broken and move on.
games.why: Genesis Rabbah keeps them side by side: dividing the world, the Temple, a woman. the silence stays open, now full of voices.

practice: Stand for a moment in the field with the two brothers, without deciding what the missing words were. Then let one conversation from your own life come to mind where the most important thing was never said out loud.
Let that silence be there; you don't have to fill it.

wordCard.voice: Stories in the gaps. Midrash, like that in Genesis Rabbah, that fills the Torah's silences with stories, often several at once. Today's word.
